def: The value of what you sold in a period, recognised when the customer receives it — not when they pay.
why: Revenue drives valuation, but it is not cash. Watch receivables grow with it.

def: Revenue minus every cost: operating costs, depreciation, interest and tax. The bottom line.
why: Profit is an accounting measure. A company can report net income and still run out of cash.

def: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: operating profit with the capital and financing decisions stripped out.
why: Lenders size loans and covenants on EBITDA; investors use it to compare businesses with different capital structures.

def: Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering it, as a share of revenue.
why: It is the money available to pay for everything else. Software keeps 80 cents of a dollar; a factory keeps 30.

def: What an office earns after its own costs, before company-wide overhead, R&D programmes, interest and tax.
why: If an office has negative contribution it destroys value every quarter it stays open, whatever it does for headline revenue.

def: The costs of running the business day to day: payroll, rent, marketing, materials.
why: They hit the income statement immediately, unlike capex.

def: Spending on long-lived assets — plant, equipment, buildings, capitalised projects. It goes on the balance sheet, not the income statement.
why: Capex costs cash today and shows up as depreciation over years, which is why fast-growing capital-heavy companies look more profitable than their bank balance suggests.

def: Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life as a non-cash expense.
why: It reduces profit without using cash, so it is added back in the cash-flow statement.

def: Costs that do not change with volume in the short run: rent, salaried staff, plant running costs.
why: High fixed costs mean idle capacity is expensive and extra volume is very profitable.

def: How much profit swings for a given change in revenue. High when most costs are fixed.
why: Automation and big plants raise it: great in a boom, brutal in a recession.

def: Cash tied up in running the business: receivables plus inventory, minus payables and deferred revenue.
why: Growth consumes working capital. A profitable manufacturer growing 50% a year can run out of cash because customers pay in 55 days and materials are bought 60 days ahead.

def: Money customers owe you for things already delivered.
why: Each sale on credit is an unsecured loan to the customer. In a recession they pay later, or not at all.

def: Materials and goods bought or made but not yet sold, carried at cost.
why: Inventory is cash sitting on a shelf. Too little loses sales; too much spoils or ties up money.

def: Money you owe suppliers for things already received.
why: Paying suppliers later is free financing — until they stop extending you credit.

def: Cash customers paid in advance for something you still owe them. A liability.
why: Subscription businesses collect before they deliver, which is why they can grow on their customers’ money.

def: What the company owns (assets) and owes (liabilities) at a moment, with the difference belonging to shareholders (equity).
why: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity. If they do not, the books are wrong.

def: Where cash came from and went in a period: operations, investing and financing.
why: It reconciles profit to cash. The gap between the two is where most surprises live.

def: How many quarters your cash lasts at the current rate of burn.
why: Insolvency is a cash event. Raise money or cut costs while you still have runway to negotiate.

def: How much cash the company consumes each quarter, after operations and capital spending.
why: Burn is fine when it buys growth investors will pay for later; it is fatal when the money stops.

def: The volume at which revenue covers all costs.
why: Below it, every quarter costs cash; above it, extra volume is mostly profit.

def: What the company is worth to buyers of its shares: enterprise value plus cash minus debt.
why: It decides how much of the company you give away when you raise money, and whether you can win.

def: Value expressed as a multiple of revenue or earnings. Growing, high-margin businesses earn higher multiples.
why: The same revenue is worth six times more in software than in logistics, because of margins, growth and capital needs.

def: The value of the operating business, regardless of how it is financed: equity value plus debt minus cash.
why: It is what an acquirer really pays for the business.

def: The reduction in existing owners’ percentage when new shares are issued.
why: Every equity raise sells part of the company. Below 50% you no longer control it.

def: Selling shares to the public for the first time and listing them on an exchange.
why: It raises money and liquidity, and puts the company under quarterly scrutiny for ever after.

def: Cash paid to shareholders out of profits.
why: Markets treat a dividend as a promise: cutting one usually hurts the share price far more than starting one helped.

def: The company buying its own shares, reducing the number outstanding.
why: It returns cash to shareholders and raises each remaining owner’s stake. Done at a high price, it destroys value.

def: How optimistic investors are, reflected in the multiples they will pay.
why: The same company is worth far more in a bull market. Raise money when sentiment is high, if you can.

def: The premium paid in an acquisition above the fair value of the assets bought.
why: It is written down if the acquired business disappoints — a public admission of overpaying.

def: The probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes.
why: A bet can have a positive expected value and still be a bad idea if losing it would end the company.

def: Debt relative to earnings, usually debt ÷ EBITDA.
why: Debt magnifies returns in good times and losses in bad ones. Lenders set covenants on it.

def: A condition in a loan agreement — maximum leverage, minimum interest cover, minimum cash. Breaking one lets the lender demand fees, a higher rate or repayment.
why: Covenants hand control to lenders before the money runs out. Watch the headroom, not just the cash.

def: A grade for how likely you are to repay debt. It sets your borrowing spread and how much anyone will lend.
why: Size, profitability, leverage and track record drive it. Every breach is remembered.

def: The price of borrowing. Floating-rate loans move with the central bank; fixed-rate loans do not.
why: Rate rises hit floating-rate borrowers immediately, and capital-heavy businesses hardest of all.

def: Debt secured on a single asset and repaid from its cash flows, typically over decades.
why: It lets an energy developer build far more than its own equity could fund — and turns rate rises into an existential risk.

def: Past losses that can be set against future profits to reduce tax.
why: They make early losses partly recoverable once the company becomes profitable.

def: The recurring swing of the economy between expansion and recession.
why: Cyclical industries (consulting, manufacturing, logistics) swing hardest; subscriptions and contracted power barely move.

def: How far the economy is running above (overheating) or below (slack) its sustainable level.
why: A positive gap pushes up wages and inflation; a negative one means weak demand and idle capacity.

def: The rate at which prices rise.
why: It is a test of pricing power: wages rise with it whether or not you can raise your prices.

def: The effect of exchange-rate moves on the value of foreign revenue and costs.
why: Local costs are a natural hedge; what is exposed is your margin, translated back home.

def: Using contracts to lock in future prices of currencies, fuel or commodities.
why: It costs a little on average and buys a narrower range of outcomes — worth most to a company that cannot afford the bad tail.

def: Your sales as a fraction of everything customers spend in a market.
why: Share moves towards the share your offer deserves — reach, quality, brand and price — at a speed set by how sticky customers are.

def: How much demand changes when price changes. An elasticity of 2 means a 10% price rise costs about 20% of volume.
why: Where elasticity is low, price rises are mostly profit; where it is high, they hand customers to rivals.

def: The ability to raise prices without losing much business.
why: It is the best single test of a strong business, and it is what inflation exposes.

def: A durable advantage that stops competitors taking your profits: scale, brand, network effects, switching costs, patents.
why: Without one, high returns attract competitors until the returns are gone.

def: Unit costs that fall as volume rises.
why: Scale is a moat in commodity industries, where the low-cost producer survives the price war.

def: A service becoming more valuable as more people or places use it.
why: In logistics, each city added makes the whole network better; that is why regional density matters.

def: What it costs a customer to change supplier — money, time, risk.
why: High switching costs make customers sticky and give suppliers pricing power. Lock-in cuts both ways.

def: Dependence on a few large customers.
why: Whoever needs the other less sets the price.

def: How much an office can deliver in a quarter: the smaller of what its people can do and what its plant can do.
why: Every office is limited by one thing at a time. Spending on anything else is wasted.

def: Output as a share of capacity.
why: Low utilisation means paying people to wait; above 95% quality slips and people burn out.

def: Revenue and cost per unit sold, before fixed costs.
why: If each unit loses money, growth makes things worse. If each unit earns, growth is the way to profit.

def: Spending to improve products and processes.
why: Technology converges on what your R&D effort can sustain: stop investing and you drift back to the pack.

def: Money already spent that cannot be recovered.
why: It should never enter a decision about what to do next. Fund the next stage only if it is worth funding on its own.

def: The right, but not the obligation, to make a future investment — like funding the next stage of a project.
why: Staging investments buys options: small bets first, bigger ones only after uncertainty is resolved.

def: Investigating an investment or acquisition before committing to it.
why: The seller always knows more than the buyer. Diligence is cheap compared with what it finds.

def: Combining an acquired business with your own: systems, people, culture.
why: Most of the value in acquisitions is made or lost after the deal closes.

def: How people feel about working for you, 0–100.
why: Low morale cuts productivity and raises attrition; layoffs leave scars that take a year to heal.

def: The share of staff who leave each period.
why: Every leaver costs recruiting fees and a quarter of lost productivity while the replacement ramps up.

def: How the company works when nobody is checking, 0–100.
why: It moves productivity, attrition and loyalty, and tilts the odds when a crisis arrives. Hiring too fast dilutes it.

def: Dependence on a few individuals whose departure would hurt the business.
why: You cannot stop people leaving; you can stop it being a crisis with successors and fair pay.

def: How well known and well regarded you are, 0–100, built region by region.
why: Brand multiplies the effect of everything else you do to win customers, and fades if you stop investing in it.

def: How customers, regulators and future employees see you, 0–100.
why: It is a reserve you draw on in a crisis. It also decides whether underwriters will take you public.

def: Environmental, social and governance performance.
why: Part cost, part option on future regulation, part brand. It is also one path to victory.
